crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Thematic Coding
children.blurb: Thematic coding is a qualitative analysis method for identifying, organizing, and interpreting recurring patterns or themes in text, interview transcripts, field notes, open ended survey responses, and other unstructured material.

children.name: Interview Transcription and Speaker Separation
children.blurb: Interview transcription and speaker separation in qualitative analysis and mixed methods refers to converting recorded interviews, focus groups, and multi-party conversations into text while attributing each utterance to the correct participant.

children.name: Finding Patterns in Lived Experience
children.blurb: Finding patterns in lived experience refers to systematic analysis of qualitative data such as interviews, diaries, open-ended survey responses, and field notes to identify recurring themes, narratives, and meanings.

children.name: Ethnographic Synthesis
children.blurb: Ethnographic synthesis brings together findings from multiple ethnographic studies to build higher-order interpretations of cultural and social phenomena.

children.name: Combining Qualitative and Quantitative Data
children.blurb: Combining qualitative and quantitative data covers research designs that bring narrative, textual, or observational material together with numeric measures, counts, or model outputs.

sections.body: Qualitative analysis and mixed methods is the branch of AI research that applies machine learning to text, audio, and field notes that do not fit neatly into numbers. Right now AI is transcribing long interviews, separating speakers in recordings, suggesting codes for themes, and clustering open ended survey answers. It is also being used to compare patterns across many transcripts and to link those patterns to survey results or demographic data. The work is practical, not theoretical, and it happens inside tools that a researcher can run on their own material. The pages here cover the actual tasks, from coding a single transcript to combining qualitative and quantitative evidence.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The state of this field is uneven. Transcription and speaker separation are now reliable enough for many research uses, though accents, overlapping speech, and poor audio still cause errors. Thematic coding is partially automated, but the codes an AI suggests often need a human to check them for meaning and context. Finding patterns in lived experience works well for surface level repetition, but it can miss irony, silence, and what people leave unsaid. Ethnographic synthesis is the least solved area, because it asks the machine to hold a whole cultural context, which current models do not do reliably. The honest limit is that AI can speed up the mechanical parts, but it cannot yet replace a researcher's judgment about what a theme means. The site's library of 135 research papers and 10,767 extracted claims shows how much evidence is still being gathered, but the field is far from a settled method.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader who wants to start with the most concrete task should go to Interview Transcription and Speaker Separation, which explains how audio becomes text and how different voices are told apart. From there, Thematic Coding shows how that text gets labeled and organized into categories. Finding Patterns in Lived Experience moves beyond single transcripts to look across many people's accounts for repeated ideas or tensions. Ethnographic Synthesis is the page for researchers who need to pull those patterns into a larger cultural or social picture, and it is the most interpretive of the group. Finally, Combining Qualitative and Quantitative Data addresses the mixed methods question directly, showing how themes from interviews can be tested against numbers from surveys or experiments. Together the pages move from raw recording to coded text, then to cross case patterns, then to synthesis, and finally to a combined analysis.
